newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: U.N. prepares for evacuation from Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.N. prepares for evacuation from Sierra Leone.

text.p: A United Nations ship arrived in Sierra Leone to evacuate U.N. staff and their dependants as foreign pressure mounted against soldiers who seized power in the West African state.
Diplomats said the El Salvatore had arrived on charter from Liberia and the evacuation of non-essential U.N. staff and their dependants was expected to start on Wednesday.
"It is not clear how they will get people to the ship," one diplomatic source said.

Three Nigerian frigates with troops docked in Freetown on Tuesday amid intense speculation that Lagos, the strongest power in the region, would intervene after the Sunday coup in which a battalion of its peacekeeping troops was drawn into fighting.

The U.S. navy helicopter ship Kearsarge with 1,200 Marines headed for Sierra Leone from the waters off Zaire, where it had been on standby for a possible evacuation during the final days of Mobutu Sese Seko's rule.
At least 40 people, including two Nigerian soldiers, were killed and twice that number wounded in fighting on Sunday, hospital sources said.

Nigeria has troops and warships in Liberia as part of the ECOMOG regional force sent there in 1990 at the height of civil war. Some units have been backing the Sierra Leone army against rebels waging an armed campaign since 1991.

An envoy of ousted President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah said the exiled leader had asked regional states to restore his government. He had also demanded sanctions against the coup leaders, Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador James Jonah said.
Jonah told reporters Kabbah had "made an appeal (to West African countries) for help to restore democracy," which could include the use of troops.
In Washington the Pentagon said the Kearsarge was steaming toward Sierra Leone but the military had received no request to evacuate Americans.

Jonah said Kabbah wanted immediate action to prevent the coup, which still faces widespread opposition, being consolidated. He emphasised that Nigerian troops were part of a West African coalition and were not acting alone.
Asked if Kabbah, now in Guinea, had asked for troops to overthrow the coup plotters, Jonah said: "If possible yes."
"What else do we have in the country? We have a bunch of corporals who opened the prisons wide open and 600 people came out, criminals, and they are roaming the streets right now."

U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said the Kearsarge would be offshore within 24 to 48 hours from its previous station off Zaire and would be "ready to conduct contingency operations if necessary". There are about 400 Americans in the capital Freetown.

Washington on Monday called for restoration of Kabbah's government, joining the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity, South Africa, Germany, Britain, France and Mali in condemning the coup led by Major Johnny Paul Koromah.
The new army rulers say they have opened land borders and air and seaports. But a dusk to dawn curfew remained in force.
Freetown residents said a new hardship in the city was an acute shortage of petrol after gas stations were looted or vandalised during the coup.
The new Armed Forces Ruling Council formed by junior officers broadcast an order for managers of National Petroleum which distributes fuel products to report to army headquarters.

Police reported protests against the coup in the southern second city of Bo, where the Kamajor militia loyal to Kabbah was ignoring an order to disband. There were also clashes between troops and Kamajors in the eastern town of Daru.

Shops, banks, schools and markets remained closed on Tuesday despite the coup leaders' appeals to people to return to work. Only a few roadside traders ventured out. The coup leaders ordered civil servants to report for work immediately.
